sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Celtic belief was pantheistic at its core. It trusted in many gods, not one. The cults were fiercely local and tribal. They stood apart from the ordered pantheons of Greece and Rome. Most Celtic deities reach us through a single text or inscription. Many belonged to a narrow district or a small folk group. In Roman days the Celts swore a famous oath. They vowed by the gods of their own people. No writing or excavation supports a ranked Irish pantheon. No supreme god ruled over a chain of lesser gods. Rome met a vast crowd of Celtic powers. It recast every one as a Roman deity. So many titles arose for Mercury and Minerva. We cannot gauge how near the Celtic gods stood to their Roman doubles. An Apollo in one town healed the sick. An Apollo elsewhere governed song and magic. Rome's renaming preserved the local cults in faint form. It also hid what the gods truly were.

okr.objective: Celtic religion was a local, tribal polytheism with no unified pantheon.
key_results: Celtic religion was pantheistic, with belief in many gods.
